line.title: Population model and fitted line
line.text: The population response equals intercept alpha plus slope beta times x plus error. The fitted value uses sample estimates a and b.

objective.title: Least-squares objective
objective.text: Residuals are observed y minus fitted y. Choose the intercept and slope that minimize the sum of squared vertical residuals.

centered-sums.title: Centered sums and least-squares coefficients
centered-sums.tex: \begin{aligned}S_{xx}&=\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2,& S_{xy}&=\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)(y_i-\bar y),\\ b&=\frac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}},&a&=\bar y-b\bar x.\end{aligned}
centered-sums.text: Sxx is the sum of squared centered predictors, Sxy is the sum of cross-products. Slope is Sxy divided by Sxx; intercept is y mean minus slope times x mean.

normal-equations.title: Normal equations and uniqueness
normal-equations.tex: \frac{\partial D}{\partial a}=-2\sum_i e_i=0,\qquad \frac{\partial D}{\partial b}=-2\sum_i x_i e_i=0
normal-equations.text: Differentiate the squared-error objective. At the minimum, residuals sum to zero and their cross-product with x is zero.

coefficient-proof.title: Deriving the slope
coefficient-proof.tex: \begin{aligned}\sum_i e_i=0&\Longrightarrow a=\bar y-b\bar x,\\ \sum_i x_i(y_i-\bar y)&=b\sum_i x_i(x_i-\bar x),\\ \sum_i x_i(x_i-\bar x)&=S_{xx},\quad\sum_i x_i(y_i-\bar y)=S_{xy}.\end{aligned}
coefficient-proof.text: Substitute the intercept expression into the second normal equation. Centered sums are zero, leaving b times Sxx equal to Sxy.

slope-covariance.title: Slope, covariance and correlation
slope-covariance.text: Using consistent covariance and variance denominators, slope equals covariance divided by x variance. When both standard deviations are positive it also equals correlation times sy over sx.

transforms.title: Effects of centering and changing units
transforms.tex: \begin{array}{c|cc}\text{New data}&\text{New slope}&\text{New intercept}\\\hline x_i^*=c x_i\;(c\ne0)&b/c&a\\y_i^*=y_i+d&b&a+d\\x_i^*=x_i-h&b&a+bh\\(x_i^*,y_i^*)=(x_i-\bar x,y_i-\bar y)&b&0\end{array}
transforms.text: Multiplying x by c divides slope by c. Adding d to y shifts the intercept by d. Centering x changes only the intercept; centering both variables gives intercept zero.

assumptions.title: Conditional Gauss–Markov assumptions
assumptions.tex: \begin{gathered}E(Y_i\mid X)=\alpha+\beta x_i,\quad E(\varepsilon_i\mid X)=0,\\\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon_i\mid X)=\sigma^2,\quad\operatorname{Cov}(\varepsilon_i,\varepsilon_j\mid X)=0\;(i\ne j),\quad S_{xx}>0.\end{gathered}
assumptions.text: Conditional on the predictor values, the mean is linear, errors have mean zero and common variance, errors are mutually uncorrelated, and the predictor varies.

mean-y.title: Correct mean and variance of the response
mean-y.tex: E(Y_i\mid X)=\alpha+\beta x_i,\qquad\operatorname{Var}(Y_i\mid X)=\sigma^2,\qquad Y_i\mid X\sim N(\alpha+\beta x_i,\sigma^2)
mean-y.text: The response mean is alpha plus beta x, not zero. Its conditional variance is sigma squared; under normal errors the response has that normal distribution.

error-residual.title: Error, residual and residual standard error
error-residual.text: A population error uses the true coefficients. A sample residual uses estimated coefficients. Divide residual sum of squares by n minus two to estimate error variance.

residual-proof.title: Residual degrees of freedom and leverage
residual-proof.text: Leverage is one over n plus squared predictor distance from the mean divided by Sxx. Leverages sum to two, leaving n minus two residual degrees of freedom.

coefficient-variance.title: Coefficient variances and covariance
coefficient-variance.text: Slope variance is sigma squared over Sxx. Intercept variance is sigma squared times one over n plus x mean squared over Sxx. Their covariance is negative x mean times sigma squared over Sxx.

coefficient-se.title: Estimated coefficient standard errors
coefficient-se.text: Replace sigma with residual standard error s. These standard errors quantify coefficient estimation uncertainty.

coefficient-tests.title: General coefficient t tests and intervals
coefficient-tests.tex: \begin{gathered}t_b=\frac{b-\beta_0}{s_b},\qquad t_a=\frac{a-\alpha_0}{s_a},\qquad T\mid H_0\sim t_{n-2},\\p_{\mathrm{two}}=2P(T_{n-2}\ge |t_{\mathrm{obs}}|),\\b\pm t_{n-2,\,1-\alpha_{\rm sig}/2}s_b,\qquad a\pm t_{n-2,\,1-\alpha_{\rm sig}/2}s_a.\end{gathered}
coefficient-tests.text: Subtract the null coefficient, divide by its standard error, and compare with t having n minus two degrees of freedom under the null. Two-sided p doubles the upper tail beyond the absolute statistic. Confidence intervals use the positive lower-tail quantile at one minus significance over two.

linear-weights.title: Linear estimator weights and covariance derivation
linear-weights.tex: \begin{gathered}b=\sum_i w_iY_i,\quad w_i=\frac{x_i-\bar x}{S_{xx}},\qquad a=\sum_i v_iY_i,\quad v_i=\frac1n-\bar xw_i,\\\sum_iw_i=0,\quad\sum_iw_i^2=\frac1{S_{xx}},\quad\sum_i v_i^2=\frac1n+\frac{\bar x^2}{S_{xx}},\\\sum_i v_iw_i=-\frac{\bar x}{S_{xx}}.\end{gathered}
linear-weights.text: Both estimates are weighted sums of responses. Uncorrelated common-variance errors turn sums of squared weights into variances and sums of weight products into covariance.

decomposition.title: Regression sum-of-squares decomposition
decomposition.tex: \begin{gathered}SST=\sum_i(y_i-\bar y)^2,\quad SSR=\sum_i(\widehat y_i-\bar y)^2,\quad SSE=\sum_i(y_i-\widehat y_i)^2,\\SST=SSR+SSE,\qquad SSR=b^2S_{xx}=\frac{S_{xy}^2}{S_{xx}}.\end{gathered}
decomposition.text: Total variation around the response mean splits into fitted-line variation and residual variation. This is the ordinary least-squares decomposition with an intercept.

decomp-proof.title: Orthogonality proof of decomposition
decomp-proof.tex: \begin{aligned}y_i-\bar y&=e_i+(\widehat y_i-\bar y),\\\sum_i e_i(\widehat y_i-\bar y)&=(a-\bar y)\sum_i e_i+b\sum_i x_i e_i=0.\end{aligned}
decomp-proof.text: Expand the squared total deviation. The cross term is zero because the normal equations make residuals orthogonal to the intercept and predictor.

r2.title: Coefficient of determination
r2.text: For simple linear OLS with an intercept and nonconstant response, R squared is the fraction of observed centered response variation explained by the fitted line, equal to squared correlation.

reg-f.title: Regression ANOVA and F test
reg-f.text: Divide regression sum of squares by one and residual sum of squares by n minus two. Their ratio has an F distribution under the zero-slope null and classical normal assumptions.

f-t-proof.title: Why F equals t squared
f-t-proof.text: Regression F equals squared slope t for the zero-slope null in the same simple model. The F upper tail corresponds to both t tails.

f-distribution.title: Independent chi-squares and expected mean squares
f-distribution.text: Under the zero-slope null, regression and error sums of squares divided by sigma squared are independent chi-squares. MSR estimates the same error variance under the null but increases in expectation with a nonzero slope.

mean-prediction.title: Mean-response standard error and confidence interval
mean-prediction.text: At predictor x0, estimate the population mean by a plus b x0. The confidence interval uses the standard error of that estimated mean.

mean-variance.title: Variance of estimated mean response
mean-variance.text: The intercept and slope estimates are correlated. Include their covariance to obtain uncertainty around the predictor mean, not around zero.

individual-prediction.title: Individual prediction and independent future error
individual-prediction.tex: \begin{gathered}Y_0=\alpha+\beta x_0+\varepsilon_0,\qquad\widehat Y_0=a+bx_0,\\\operatorname{Var}(Y_0-\widehat Y_0\mid X,x_0)=\sigma^2(1+h_0),\\\widehat Y_0\pm t_{n-2,\,1-\alpha_{\rm sig}/2}\,s\sqrt{1+h_0}.\end{gathered}
individual-prediction.text: A new individual response includes an independent future error. The prediction interval adds one times the error variance to the uncertainty in the estimated mean.

prediction-proof.title: Prediction-error variance derivation
prediction-proof.text: Independence of the new error and fitting data removes the covariance term. Add the new observation variance and fitted-mean variance.

depth-slope-weights.title: A slope as a weighted sum of responses
depth-slope-weights.text: For fixed spending values, the slope is a weighted sum of responses. The eight weights are negative 7, negative 5, negative 3, negative 1, 1, 3, 5 and 7, all divided by 84. They sum to zero; their products with x sum to one; their squares sum to one over 42.

depth-slope-unbiased.title: Why the slope is unbiased under the model
depth-slope-unbiased.text: Substitute the population model into the weighted sum. The intercept term cancels, the slope term equals beta, and the remaining weighted errors have conditional expectation zero. Hence the slope estimator has conditional expectation beta.

depth-mean-covariance.title: Keep covariance when calculating mean-response uncertainty
depth-mean-covariance.text: Estimated variance of the intercept is 459 over 784, slope variance is 9 over 392 and their covariance is negative 81 over 784. Variance of a plus 4.5 b includes both variance terms and twice 4.5 times the covariance. The result is 27 over 224, giving standard error about 0.3472 tens of orders.

depth-normal-balance.title: Expand the intercept balance
depth-normal-balance.tex: \begin{aligned}0&=\sum_i(y_i-a-bx_i)\\&=\sum_i y_i-na-b\sum_i x_i,\\0&=\bar y-a-b\bar x,\\a&=\bar y-b\bar x.\end{aligned}
depth-normal-balance.text: The sum of residuals is the sum of y minus n times a minus b times the sum of x. Divide by n: zero equals y mean minus a minus b times x mean. Therefore a equals y mean minus b times x mean.

depth-normal-centering.title: Show the cancellation that creates centered sums
depth-normal-centering.tex: \begin{aligned}\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)&=0,&\sum_i(y_i-\bar y)&=0,\\\sum_i x_i(y_i-\bar y)&=S_{xy}+\bar x\sum_i(y_i-\bar y)\\&=S_{xy},\\\sum_i x_i(x_i-\bar x)&=S_{xx}+\bar x\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)\\&=S_{xx},\\0&=S_{xy}-bS_{xx},\\b&=\frac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}}\quad(S_{xx}>0).\end{aligned}
depth-normal-centering.text: Deviations from each mean sum to zero. The sum of x times centered y is Sxy plus x mean times the sum of centered y, so it equals Sxy. The sum of x times centered x similarly equals Sxx. The second balance becomes zero equals Sxy minus b times Sxx. If Sxx is positive, b equals Sxy divided by Sxx.

depth-normal-numbers.title: Solve the two equations for the eight market-weeks
depth-normal-numbers.text: The data give 8 a plus 36 b equals 140 and 36 a plus 204 b equals 711. The first gives a equals 17.5 minus 4.5 b. Substituting into the second gives 42 b equals 81. Thus b is 27 over 14 and a is 247 over 28.

depth-normal-minimum.title: Every other line has a larger squared-error total
depth-normal-minimum.text: Let a star and b star be the fitted coefficients. Changing them by u and v increases the squared-error total by the sum of squared quantities u plus v x. This is n times the square of u plus v x mean, plus v squared times Sxx. When Sxx is positive, the increase is positive unless u and v are both zero.
